findings.title: Blocked-email matching is case- and whitespace-sensitive, allowing bypass
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` looks up the address with an exact `where(email: email)` match, and `BlockedEmail` does not normalize email on write; the migration's unique index on `email` also does not enforce case-insensitive uniqueness. The User model/controller do not downcase or strip `params[:email]` before validation, so an address blocked as `bad@spam.com` is not matched when submitted as `Bad@Spam.com` or with surrounding whitespace, and the account can still be created. Normalize email on insert and lookup (e.g. `strip.downcase`), make uniqueness/index case-insensitive, and add a regression spec for mixed-case input.

findings.title: Blocked-email statistics are updated during validation, causing duplicate and racy increments
findings.body: `should_block?` increments `match_count` and saves the record every time it is called, but it is called from `EmailValidator`, so every validation pass mutates the database. In `UsersController#create` the code calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, which re-runs validations, so one blocked signup attempt increments `match_count` at least twice; every additional `valid?` call increments it again. The `match_count += 1`/`save` sequence is also a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent attempts can lose increments. Move the statistics update out of the validation path or use an atomic update, and avoid validating the same user twice in the controller.

findings.title: Domain whitelist regex is unanchored and can be bypassed
findings.body: The restriction regex is built as `@(#{domains})` with no end anchor. If `email_domains_whitelist` is `example.com`, the address `user@example.com.attacker.tld` matches because the string contains `@example.com`, even though the actual domain is under `attacker.tld`. Since this validator is the only server-side domain check, an attacker controlling `attacker.tld` can satisfy a whitelist they should not satisfy; blacklist matching can also produce false positives. Anchor the domain pattern at the end (and add specs covering lookalike domains).
